question: What is the mass of 0.25 mol of CO2? (C = 12, O = 16)
why: Molar mass of CO2 is 44 g/mol, so 0.25 x 44 = 11 g.

question: How many significant figures are there in 0.00450?
why: Leading zeros do not count; 4, 5 and the trailing 0 after the decimal digits do, giving three.

question: What is the mass percentage of carbon in acetic acid, CH3COOH? (H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
why: Molar mass is 60 g/mol and carbon contributes 2 x 12 = 24 g, so 24/60 = 40%.

question: 9.8 g of H2SO4 (molar mass 98 g/mol) is dissolved in water to make 500 mL of solution. What is its molarity?
why: Moles = 9.8/98 = 0.1 mol; volume is 0.5 L, so 0.1/0.5 = 0.2 M.

question: For 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, 4 g of H2 is mixed with 48 g of O2. What mass of water forms at most? (H = 1, O = 16)
why: H2 is 2 mol and needs only 1 mol O2 (of the 1.5 mol present), so H2 limits: 2 mol water = 36 g.

question: A compound has 40% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O by mass and a molar mass of 90 g/mol. What is its molecular formula? (H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
why: The ratio gives empirical formula CH2O (mass 30); 90/30 = 3, so the molecular formula is C3H6O3.

question: How many neutrons are there in an atom of sodium-23 (atomic number 11)?
why: Neutrons = mass number - atomic number = 23 - 11 = 12.

question: Which quantum number decides the shape of an orbital?
why: l = 0, 1, 2 gives s, p, d shapes; n gives size and energy, m gives orientation.

question: What is the maximum number of electrons that can be accommodated in the shell with n = 3?
why: A shell holds 2n^2 electrons, and 2 x 9 = 18.

question: Which is the correct ground-state electronic configuration of chromium (Z = 24)?
why: Half-filled 3d5 with one electron in 4s is extra stable, so one 4s electron moves to 3d.

question: An electron (mass 9.109 x 10^-31 kg) moves at 1.0 x 10^6 m/s. What is its de Broglie wavelength? (h = 6.626 x 10^-34 J s)
How many radial nodes and angular nodes does a 4p orbital have?
why: Radial nodes = n - l - 1 = 4 - 1 - 1 = 2; angular nodes = l = 1.

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: In which group and period is the element with atomic number 20 placed?
why: Z = 20 is [Ar] 4s2: two valence electrons (group 2) in the fourth shell (period 4).

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: Which of these has the largest atomic radius?
why: Across a period nuclear charge rises and radius shrinks, so the first element, Na, is largest.

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: Which of these isoelectronic species has the largest radius: O2-, F-, Na+, Mg2+?
why: All have 10 electrons; the lowest nuclear charge (8) pulls them least, so O2- is largest.

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: Which of these has the highest first ionisation enthalpy?
why: N has a stable half-filled 2p3 shell, so its first ionisation enthalpy exceeds that of O, Be and B.

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: Which halogen has the most negative electron gain enthalpy?
why: F is so small that added electrons feel strong repulsion, so Cl gains an electron most exothermically.

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: An element has first and second ionisation enthalpies of 520 and 7298 kJ/mol. To which group does it most likely belong?
why: A huge jump after the first removal means a noble-gas core is being broken, so one valence electron: group 1.

question: What is the shape of the NH3 molecule?
why: Three bond pairs and one lone pair on N give a pyramidal shape.

question: What is the bond order of the O2 molecule?
why: Bonding electrons 10, antibonding 6, so (10 - 6)/2 = 2.

question: What is the shape of the XeF4 molecule?
why: Xe has four bond pairs and two lone pairs, placed opposite each other, giving a square planar molecule.

question: What is the bond order of N2+? (N2 has bond order 3 with 10 bonding and 4 antibonding electrons)
why: Removing one bonding electron gives (9 - 4)/2 = 2.5.

question: Which of these diatomic species is paramagnetic?
why: B2 has two unpaired electrons in degenerate pi orbitals; N2, C2 and F2 have all electrons paired.

question: What is the shape of XeF2 and how many lone pairs are on the xenon atom?
why: Five electron pairs form a trigonal bipyramid; the three lone pairs sit in the equatorial plane, leaving F-Xe-F linear.

question: A closed system can exchange which of these with its surroundings?
why: A closed system has a fixed amount of matter but can exchange heat and work.

question: Which of these is a state function?
why: Enthalpy depends only on the state of the system; heat and work depend on the path.

question: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on the surroundings. What is the change in its internal energy?
why: Delta U = q + w = 500 + (-200) = +300 J, since work done by the system is negative.

question: For N2(g) + 3H2(g) -> 2NH3(g) at 300 K, what is (Delta H - Delta U)? (R = 8.314 J/K/mol)
why: Delta n(gas) = 2 - 4 = -2, so Delta H - Delta U = -2 x 8.314 x 300 = -4988 J.

question: Delta H is -393.5 kJ/mol for C(graphite) + O2 -> CO2 and -283.0 kJ/mol for CO + 1/2 O2 -> CO2. What is Delta H for C(graphite) + 1/2 O2 -> CO?
why: Subtract the second equation from the first: -393.5 - (-283.0) = -110.5 kJ/mol.

question: A process has Delta H = +40 kJ/mol and Delta S = +125 J/K/mol. Above what temperature does it become spontaneous?
why: Delta G = 0 at T = Delta H/Delta S = 40000/125 = 320 K; remember to convert kJ to J.

question: What is the expression of Kc for N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g)?
why: Products go in the numerator and reactants in the denominator, each raised to its coefficient.

question: For N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g), what happens to the equilibrium when pressure is raised at constant temperature?
a: It shifts towards N2 and H2
why: Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles, 2 versus 4.

question: What is the pH of 0.001 M NaOH solution at 25 C?
why: [OH-] = 1e-3, so pOH = 3 and pH = 14 - 3 = 11.

question: For N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g), Kc = 0.02 mol/L at 400 K. What is Kp in atm? (R = 0.0821 L atm/K/mol)
Ksp of AgCl is 1.8 x 10^-10. What is its approximate solubility in 0.1 M NaCl?
why: Common ion Cl- is 0.1 M, so s = Ksp/0.1 = 1.8e-9 M.

question: A buffer has 0.2 M sodium acetate and 0.1 M acetic acid (pKa = 4.76). What is its pH?
why: pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]) = 4.76 + log 2 = 5.06.

question: What is the oxidation number of sulphur in H2SO4?
In Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu, which species is the reducing agent?
why: Zn loses electrons (is oxidised) and so reduces Cu2+.

question: What is the average oxidation number of sulphur in Na2S4O6?
In acidic medium MnO4- is reduced to Mn2+. How many electrons does each MnO4- gain?
why: Mn goes from +7 to +2, a gain of 5 electrons.

question: In acidic medium, how many moles of KMnO4 are needed to oxidise 1 mol of FeC2O4 completely to Fe3+ and CO2?
why: Fe2+ gives 1 e- and C2O4 2- gives 2 e-, total 3; each MnO4- takes 5, so 3/5 = 0.6 mol.

question: Which of these is a disproportionation reaction?
why: Oxygen in H2O2 (-1) goes to both -2 in water and 0 in O2, so one element is both oxidised and reduced.

chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
question: What is the IUPAC name of CH3-CH(CH3)-CH3?
why: The longest chain has three carbons (propane) with a methyl on carbon 2.

chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
question: What is the hybridisation of each carbon atom in ethene, CH2=CH2?
why: Each carbon has three sigma bonds and one pi bond, so it uses three sp2 orbitals.

chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
question: Which carbocation is the most stable?
why: More alkyl groups give more +I effect and hyperconjugation, so the tertiary one is most stable.

chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
question: How many structural isomers does pentane, C5H12, have (including pentane itself)?
why: Pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane.

chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
question: What is the IUPAC name of CH3-CH(CH3)-CH2-CH(C2H5)-CH3?
why: The longest chain is six carbons; numbering from the end giving lowest locants places methyls at 2 and 4.

chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
question: In the Kjeldahl method, 1.0 g of an organic compound releases ammonia that neutralises 15 mL of 0.5 M H2SO4. What is the percentage of nitrogen? (N = 14)
why: Acid = 0.0075 mol; each mol H2SO4 neutralises 2 mol NH3, so N = 0.015 mol = 0.21 g in 1.0 g.

question: What are the products of complete combustion of methane?
why: With excess oxygen, carbon forms CO2 and hydrogen forms water.

question: What is the general formula of alkynes?
why: Alkynes have a triple bond, so two fewer hydrogens than alkenes.

question: What is the major product when propene reacts with HBr?
why: H adds to the carbon with more hydrogens, and Br goes to the more substituted carbon.

question: Ethyne passed through a red-hot iron tube at 873 K gives mainly which compound?
why: Three ethyne molecules polymerise (cyclic trimerisation) into benzene.

question: A mixture of CH3Br and C2H5Br is heated with sodium in dry ether. How many different alkanes can form?
why: Ethane (CH3-CH3), propane (CH3-C2H5) and butane (C2H5-C2H5) all form.

question: Which of these species is aromatic?
why: The anion is planar, cyclic and has 6 pi electrons (4n + 2); the others have 4n or are non-planar.

question: How many moles are there in 36 g of water? (H = 1, O = 16)
why: Molar mass of H2O is 18 g/mol, so 36 / 18 = 2 mol.

question: How many atoms are present in 1 mole of oxygen gas, O2?
why: One mole of O2 has 6.022 x 10^23 molecules and each molecule has 2 atoms, so 1.204 x 10^24 atoms.

question: Which of these is a mixture and not a pure substance?
why: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc mixed in varying proportions. The other three are pure substances.

question: Water from a river and from a rain-water tank, once purified, both contain hydrogen and oxygen in the mass ratio 1 : 8. Which law does this show?
why: A pure compound always has its elements in a fixed mass ratio, whatever its source. That is the law of definite proportions.

question: What is the SI unit of the amount of a substance?
why: The mole is the SI base unit for amount of substance.

question: What is the molar mass of ammonia, NH3? (N = 14, H = 1)
What is the mass of 3.011 x 10^23 molecules of CO2? (C = 12, O = 16)
why: 3.011 x 10^23 molecules is 0.5 mol, and 0.5 x 44 g/mol = 22 g.

question: A hydrocarbon contains 85.7% carbon and 14.3% hydrogen by mass. What is its empirical formula? (C = 12, H = 1)
why: C : H = 85.7/12 : 14.3/1 = 7.14 : 14.3 = 1 : 2, so the empirical formula is CH2.

question: 4 g of NaOH (molar mass 40 g/mol) is dissolved in water to make 250 mL of solution. What is its molarity?
why: Moles = 4/40 = 0.1 mol. Molarity = 0.1 mol / 0.25 L = 0.4 M. Using 250 mL as litres is the common slip.

question: What volume does 8.8 g of CO2 occupy at STP? (Molar volume = 22.4 L/mol; C = 12, O = 16)
100 mL of 2 M HCl is diluted with water to a total volume of 400 mL. What is the new molarity?
10 g of sodium chloride is dissolved in 90 g of water. What is the mass percentage of NaCl in the solution?
why: Mass percent uses the mass of the whole solution: 10 / (10 + 90) x 100 = 10%.

question: 28 g of N2 is mixed with 9 g of H2 and they react completely to form NH3 in N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3. What mass of NH3 forms? (N = 14, H = 1)
why: N2 is 1 mol and H2 is 4.5 mol. 1 mol N2 needs only 3 mol H2, so N2 is limiting and gives 2 mol NH3 = 34 g.

question: A compound has 92.3% carbon and 7.7% hydrogen by mass and its molar mass is 78 g/mol. What is its molecular formula? (C = 12, H = 1)
why: Empirical formula is CH (mass 13). 78 / 13 = 6, so the molecular formula is C6H6.

question: 10 g of an impure limestone sample is heated strongly and gives 2.2 g of CO2 (CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2). What is the percentage of pure CaCO3 in the sample? (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
why: 2.2 g CO2 is 0.05 mol, so 0.05 mol CaCO3 = 5 g was present. 5/10 x 100 = 50%.

question: 18 g of glucose (molar mass 180 g/mol) is dissolved in 180 g of water (molar mass 18 g/mol). What is the mole fraction of glucose?
why: Moles: glucose 0.1, water 10. Mole fraction = 0.1 / 10.1 = 0.0099.

question: How many moles of O2 are needed to burn 4.4 g of propane, C3H8, completely? (C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O; C = 12, H = 1)
why: 4.4 g is 0.1 mol of propane, and each mole needs 5 mol O2, so 0.5 mol.

question: 300 mL of 0.5 M HCl is mixed with 200 mL of 1.0 M HCl. What is the molarity of the mixture, assuming volumes add?
why: Moles = 0.15 + 0.20 = 0.35 mol in 0.5 L, so 0.7 M. Simply averaging 0.5 and 1.0 ignores the different volumes.

question: Which subatomic particle has no charge and a mass of about 1 u?
why: The neutron is neutral and has a mass close to that of a proton, about 1 u.

question: How many electrons are there in an Al3+ ion? (Atomic number of Al = 13)
why: Al has 13 electrons; losing 3 leaves 10.

question: What is the maximum number of electrons that a d subshell can hold?
why: A d subshell has 5 orbitals, each holding 2 electrons, so 10.

question: In a multi-electron atom, which orbital has the lowest energy?
why: Among these, 3s is lowest: 3s < 3p < 4s < 3d.

question: How many orbitals are there in a p subshell?
why: A p subshell has l = 1, so it has 2l + 1 = 3 orbitals.

question: Which principle states that no two electrons in an atom can have the same set of all four quantum numbers?
why: This is the Pauli exclusion principle; it limits each orbital to two electrons of opposite spin.

question: How many unpaired electrons are there in the Fe3+ ion? (Atomic number of Fe = 26)
why: Fe3+ is [Ar]3d5, with all five d electrons unpaired.

question: What is the wavelength of light of frequency 6 x 10^14 Hz? (c = 3 x 10^8 m/s)
why: Wavelength = c / frequency = 3 x 10^8 / 6 x 10^14 = 5 x 10^-7 m = 500 nm.

question: Which set of quantum numbers (n, l, m) is NOT allowed for an electron?
why: l can only go from 0 to n - 1. For n = 2, l = 2 is not possible.

question: What is the energy of the electron in the n = 2 orbit of a hydrogen atom? (Energy for n = 1 is -13.6 eV)
How many electrons in a chlorine atom (Z = 17) occupy p orbitals?
why: Cl is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5. p electrons = 6 + 5 = 11.

question: How many orbitals are there in the shell with n = 3?
why: The number of orbitals in a shell is n^2 = 9.

question: What is the radius of the third Bohr orbit of Li2+? (Radius of first orbit of hydrogen = 52.9 pm; Z = 3)
why: r = 52.9 x n^2 / Z = 52.9 x 9 / 3 = 158.7 pm. Forgetting Z gives 476.1 pm.

question: Using the Rydberg constant 1.097 x 10^7 m^-1, what is the wavelength of the line when a hydrogen electron falls from n = 3 to n = 2?
why: 1/wavelength = 1.097 x 10^7 x (1/4 - 1/9) = 1.52 x 10^6 m^-1, giving 656 nm (red Balmer line).

question: What is the de Broglie wavelength of a 0.1 kg ball moving at 10 m/s? (h = 6.626 x 10^-34 J s)
why: Momentum is 0.1 x 10 = 1 kg m/s, so wavelength = 6.626 x 10^-34 / 1 = 6.6 x 10^-34 m, far too small to detect.

question: Hydrogen atoms are excited to the n = 5 level. What is the maximum number of different spectral lines possible as they return to lower levels?
why: Number of lines = n(n - 1)/2 = 5 x 4 / 2 = 10.

question: What is the ionisation energy of the He+ ion in its ground state? (Ionisation energy of H = 13.6 eV)
why: Energy scales as Z^2, so 13.6 x 4 = 54.4 eV.

question: The threshold frequency of a metal is 5 x 10^14 Hz. Light of 8 x 10^14 Hz falls on it. What is the maximum kinetic energy of an ejected electron? (h = 6.626 x 10^-34 J s)

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: To which block does an element with outer configuration 3s2 3p4 belong?
why: The last electron enters a p subshell, so it is a p-block element (sulphur).

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: In which group is the element with atomic number 10 (neon) placed?
why: Neon has a complete octet and is a noble gas in group 18.

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: Which element is the most electronegative?
why: Fluorine has the highest electronegativity (4.0 on the Pauling scale).

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: What is the general outer electronic configuration of alkali metals?
why: Alkali metals (group 1) have one electron in the outer s orbital.

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: How does atomic radius change from left to right across a period?
d: It first increases and then decreases
why: Nuclear charge increases while the shell stays the same, so electrons are pulled closer and radius falls.

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: Which of these elements is a metalloid?
why: Silicon, like germanium and arsenic, shows both metallic and non-metallic properties.

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: Which has the higher first ionisation enthalpy, beryllium (Z = 4) or boron (Z = 5), and why?
a: Be, because its 2s subshell is full and more stable than the 2p electron of B
b: B, because it has more protons
c: Be, because it is larger than B
d: B, because its 2p electron is closer to the nucleus
why: The 2p electron of boron is higher in energy and slightly shielded by 2s, so it is easier to remove than a 2s electron of Be.

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: Which element shows a diagonal relationship with beryllium?
why: Be and Al have similar charge to size ratios, so they resemble each other (for example both have amphoteric oxides).

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: Zirconium and hafnium have almost the same atomic radius. What is the reason?
why: Poor shielding by 4f electrons between Zr and Hf shrinks Hf, cancelling the expected size increase.

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: An element has the configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s1. In which period and group is it placed?
why: The highest shell is n = 4, so period 4, and one outer electron puts it in group 1 (potassium).

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: Which of these oxides is the most basic?
why: Basic character of oxides falls across a period: Na2O is strongly basic, Al2O3 is amphoteric and SiO2 is acidic.

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: How many elements are there in the fourth period?
why: The fourth period fills 4s, 3d and 4p, giving 2 + 10 + 6 = 18 elements.

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: An element has successive ionisation enthalpies (kJ/mol) of 578, 1817, 2745 and 11578. To which group does it most likely belong?
why: The big jump comes after the third value, so three valence electrons are easy to remove: group 13.

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: Arrange the oxides Na2O, MgO, P2O5 and SO3 in increasing order of acidic character.
why: Acidic character increases with non-metallic character across the period, and SO3 is the most acidic of these.

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: Assertion: The second ionisation enthalpy of sodium is much higher than its first. Reason: Na+ has a stable noble gas configuration. Which option is correct?
a: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion
b: Both are true but the reason does not explain the assertion
c: Assertion is true but the reason is false
d: Assertion is false but the reason is true
why: Removing an electron from the noble-gas-like Na+ breaks a stable octet, which is why the second value is so high.

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: Which of these elements has the highest second ionisation enthalpy?
why: After losing one electron, Na+ has a neon configuration, so removing the second electron is very difficult.

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: Aluminium's first ionisation enthalpy is lower than magnesium's. What is the best reason?
a: Al's outer electron is in a 3p orbital, higher in energy and shielded by 3s
d: Al has a higher nuclear charge, which weakens the hold on electrons
why: The 3p electron of Al is easier to remove than the full 3s electron of Mg, in spite of Al having more protons.

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
question: If element 119 were discovered, in which group, period and block would it be placed?
why: Element 118 completes period 7, so 119 starts period 8 with one s electron, like the alkali metals.

question: Which type of bond is formed by the complete transfer of electrons from one atom to another?
why: Complete transfer of electrons forms ions that attract each other: an ionic bond.

question: What is the shape of the methane molecule, CH4?
why: Four bond pairs and no lone pair give a tetrahedral shape with 109.5 degree angles.

question: What is the hybridisation of carbon in methane?
why: One s and three p orbitals mix to give four sp3 hybrid orbitals.

question: What is the shape of the BF3 molecule?
why: Boron has three bond pairs and no lone pair (sp2), so the molecule is flat with 120 degree angles.

question: How many pi bonds are there in a nitrogen molecule, N2?
why: N2 has a triple bond: one sigma and two pi bonds.

question: Which of these molecules is linear?
why: Carbon in CO2 is sp hybridised with no lone pair, so O=C=O is linear.

question: What is the bond order of the O2- (superoxide) ion?
why: O2- has 10 bonding and 7 antibonding electrons, so the bond order is (10 - 7) / 2 = 1.5.

question: What is the hybridisation of phosphorus in PCl5?
why: Five bond pairs need five hybrid orbitals from one s, three p and one d orbital.

question: Which of these molecules has a zero dipole moment?
why: The four C-Cl dipoles in tetrahedral CCl4 cancel each other.

question: What is the shape of the SO2 molecule?
why: Sulphur has two bond pairs and one lone pair (sp2), which gives a bent shape.

question: Which gives the correct order of H-X-H bond angles?
why: Lone pairs squeeze bond angles: no lone pair in CH4 (109.5), one in NH3 (107), two in H2O (104.5).

question: How many sigma and pi bonds are there in propyne, CH3-C#CH?
why: There are 4 C-H, 1 C-C and 1 sigma of the triple bond: 6 sigma. The triple bond also has 2 pi bonds.

question: Which statement about the C2 molecule is correct according to molecular orbital theory?
why: C2 has 8 bonding and 4 antibonding electrons (bond order 2), and both pi bonding orbitals hold paired electrons, so it is diamagnetic.

question: Arrange O2+, O2, O2- and O2(2-) in order of increasing bond length.
why: Bond orders are 2.5, 2, 1.5 and 1. Higher bond order means a shorter bond.

question: What is the shape of the ClF3 molecule?
why: Chlorine has three bond pairs and two lone pairs (five electron pairs); the lone pairs sit in the equatorial plane, leaving a T shape.

question: What is the shape of the ICl4- ion?
why: Iodine has four bond pairs and two lone pairs (six pairs, sp3d2), and the lone pairs sit opposite each other, giving a square planar ion.

question: Assertion: NH3 has a larger dipole moment than NF3. Reason: In NF3 the N-F bond dipoles oppose the dipole of the lone pair. Which option is correct?
a: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion
b: Both are true but the reason does not explain the assertion
c: Assertion is true but the reason is false
d: Assertion is false but the reason is true
why: In NH3 the N-H dipoles point the same way as the lone pair, but in NF3 the N-F dipoles point the opposite way and partly cancel it.

question: What is the shape of XeO3 and how many lone pairs are on xenon?
why: Xe has 8 valence electrons; three are used in bonds to O, leaving one lone pair and a pyramidal shape.

question: Which of these is an intensive property?
why: Intensive properties do not depend on the amount of matter. Temperature is one; mass, volume and enthalpy are extensive.

question: What is the sign of the enthalpy change for an exothermic reaction?
why: An exothermic reaction releases heat to the surroundings, so delta H is negative.

question: What does an isolated system exchange with its surroundings?
why: By definition an isolated system exchanges neither matter nor energy.

question: What is the standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its most stable standard state, such as O2(g)?
why: The formation of an element from itself involves no change, so it is zero by convention.

question: A system absorbs 200 J of heat and does no work. What is the change in its internal energy?
What happens to the entropy of a substance when ice melts to water?
why: Liquid water is more disordered than ice, so entropy increases.

question: For a reaction, delta H = -50 kJ/mol and delta S = -100 J/K/mol. What is delta G at 300 K?
why: delta G = delta H - T delta S = -50 - (300 x -0.100) = -50 + 30 = -20 kJ/mol. Note delta S must be in kJ.

question: How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of 200 g of water from 20 C to 50 C? (Specific heat = 4.18 J/g/C)
A gas expands from 1 L to 6 L against a constant external pressure of 2 atm. What is the work done on the gas? (1 L atm = 101.3 J)
why: w = -p delta V = -2 x 5 = -10 L atm = -1013 J. Work is negative because the gas expands.

question: Given N2 + O2 -> 2NO, delta H = +180.6 kJ and 2NO + O2 -> 2NO2, delta H = -114.2 kJ, what is delta H for N2 + 2O2 -> 2NO2?
why: By Hess's law, add the two steps: 180.6 + (-114.2) = +66.4 kJ.

question: Bond enthalpies (kJ/mol): H-H 436, Cl-Cl 243, H-Cl 431. What is delta H for H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl?
why: Bonds broken: 436 + 243 = 679. Bonds formed: 2 x 431 = 862. delta H = 679 - 862 = -183 kJ.

question: For which combination of delta H and delta S is a reaction spontaneous at all temperatures?
a: delta H positive, delta S negative
b: delta H positive, delta S positive
c: delta H negative, delta S positive
d: delta H negative, delta S negative
why: delta G = delta H - T delta S is negative at every T only when delta H < 0 and delta S > 0.

question: For C2H5OH(l) + 3O2(g) -> 2CO2(g) + 3H2O(l) at 298 K, what is (delta H - delta U)? (R = 8.314 J/K/mol)
why: Gas moles change from 3 to 2, so delta n = -1 and delta H - delta U = delta n RT = -8.314 x 298 = -2478 J.

question: Enthalpies of combustion (kJ/mol): graphite -393.5, H2 -285.8, CH4 -890.3. What is the enthalpy of formation of CH4?
At 298 K a reaction has standard Gibbs energy change of -5.7 kJ/mol. Approximately what is its equilibrium constant? (R = 8.314 J/K/mol)
2 mol of an ideal gas expands isothermally to double its volume. What is the entropy change? (R = 8.314 J/K/mol, ln 2 = 0.693)
why: delta S = nR ln(V2/V1) = 2 x 8.314 x 0.693 = 11.5 J/K. Entropy rises with volume.

question: A bomb calorimeter with heat capacity 5.0 kJ/K shows a 2.4 K rise when 1.0 g of a compound (molar mass 180 g/mol) is burnt. What is the heat released per mole?
why: q = 5.0 x 2.4 = 12 kJ per gram. Per mole = 12 x 180 = 2160 kJ.

question: For N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3, delta H = -92.2 kJ and delta S = -198.7 J/K. Above roughly which temperature does the reaction stop being spontaneous?
why: delta G = 0 when T = delta H / delta S = 92200 / 198.7 = 464 K. Above this, -T delta S outweighs delta H.

question: What is the pH of 0.01 M HCl solution?
why: HCl is a strong acid, so [H+] = 0.01 M = 10^-2 and pH = 2.

topic: Law of chemical equilibrium, Kc and Kp
question: Which one factor changes the value of the equilibrium constant Kc?
why: Kc depends only on temperature (for a given reaction).

question: What is the effect of a catalyst on the position of an equilibrium?
why: A catalyst speeds up forward and backward reactions equally, so it only helps to reach equilibrium faster.

question: What is the pH of pure water at 25 C?
why: At 25 C, [H+] = [OH-] = 10^-7 M in pure water.

question: What is the conjugate base of NH4+?
why: Removing a proton from NH4+ gives NH3.

question: In N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3, what happens if more N2 is added at constant temperature?
why: Adding reactant is opposed by shifting the reaction forward to use some of it up.

topic: Law of chemical equilibrium, Kc and Kp
question: For N2O4 <=> 2NO2, Kc = 0.25 at a given temperature. What is Kc for 2NO2 <=> N2O4 at the same temperature?
why: Reversing the reaction inverts the constant: 1 / 0.25 = 4.

question: What is the pH of a solution in which [H+] = 5 x 10^-4 M? (log 5 = 0.70)

topic: Law of chemical equilibrium, Kc and Kp
question: For N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3, which relation between Kp and Kc is correct?
why: Kp = Kc (RT)^(delta n) with delta n = 2 - 4 = -2.

topic: Law of chemical equilibrium, Kc and Kp
question: For A <=> B, Kc = 4. Starting with 1.0 M A and no B, what is the equilibrium concentration of B?
why: x / (1 - x) = 4 gives x = 0.8 M.

question: The salt AB2 has Ksp = 3.2 x 10^-11. What is its solubility in mol/L?
why: Ksp = 4s^3, so s^3 = 8 x 10^-12 and s = 2 x 10^-4 mol/L.

question: A 0.1 M solution of a weak monobasic acid has pH 3. What is its Ka?
What is the approximate pH of 0.1 M NH3 solution? (Kb = 1.8 x 10^-5; log 1.34 = 0.13)
50 mL of 0.2 M HCl is mixed with 50 mL of 0.1 M NaOH. What is the pH of the mixture?
why: Moles HCl = 0.010, NaOH = 0.005, leaving 0.005 mol H+ in 0.1 L, so 0.05 M and pH = 1.30.

topic: Law of chemical equilibrium, Kc and Kp
question: 1 mol each of H2 and I2 are heated in a 1 L vessel and 1.6 mol of HI is present at equilibrium for H2 + I2 <=> 2HI. What is Kc?
A 1 L buffer has 0.10 mol acetic acid and 0.10 mol sodium acetate (pKa = 4.76). What is its pH after 0.01 mol HCl is added? (log 0.818 = -0.087)
why: HCl converts 0.01 mol acetate to acetic acid: acetate 0.09, acid 0.11. pH = 4.76 + log(0.09/0.11) = 4.67.

topic: Law of chemical equilibrium, Kc and Kp
question: PCl5 <=> PCl3 + Cl2 is 20% dissociated at a total pressure of 1 atm. What is Kp?
What is the approximate pH of 0.1 M sodium acetate solution? (pKa of acetic acid = 4.76)
why: For a salt of a weak acid and strong base, pH = 7 + 1/2 (pKa + log C) = 7 + 0.5 (4.76 - 1) = 8.88.

question: What is the oxidation number of chromium in K2Cr2O7?
What is the oxidation number of oxygen in hydrogen peroxide, H2O2?
why: In peroxides, the O-O bond makes the oxidation number of oxygen -1.

question: Oxidation is defined as which of these?
why: Oxidation is loss of electrons (an increase in oxidation number).

question: What is the oxidation number of chlorine in HClO4?
In 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl, what is the role of Cl2?
why: Cl2 gains electrons (0 to -1), so it is reduced and acts as the oxidising agent.

question: What is the oxidation number of nitrogen in NH3?
What is the average oxidation number of sulphur in the thiosulphate ion, S2O3(2-)?
Which of these reactions is NOT a redox reaction?
why: In the precipitation reaction no element changes its oxidation number.

question: How many electrons are needed to convert one Cr2O7(2-) ion to two Cr3+ ions?
why: Each Cr goes from +6 to +3, gaining 3 electrons, so 2 x 3 = 6.

question: When MnO4- is reduced to MnO2, how many electrons does each MnO4- gain?
why: Mn changes from +7 to +4, gaining 3 electrons.

question: Which of these can act only as an oxidising agent?
why: Nitrogen in HNO3 is at its maximum oxidation state +5, so it can only decrease. The others can also be oxidised.

question: What is the oxidation number of carbon in methanol, CH3OH?
In acidic medium MnO4- is reduced to Mn2+ and Fe2+ is oxidised to Fe3+. How many moles of Fe2+ does 1 mole of MnO4- oxidise?
why: MnO4- gains 5 electrons and each Fe2+ loses 1, so 5 Fe2+ are oxidised.

question: How many mL of 0.02 M KMnO4 are needed in acidic medium to oxidise 25 mL of 0.1 M FeSO4?
In 3Cl2 + 6NaOH -> 5NaCl + NaClO3 + 3H2O, how many electrons are transferred in total?
why: Of the six Cl atoms, five go 0 to -1 (gaining 5 electrons) and one goes 0 to +5 (losing 5 electrons). So 5 are transferred.

question: What is the equivalent mass of KMnO4 (molar mass 158 g/mol) as an oxidising agent in acidic medium?
why: In acid, MnO4- gains 5 electrons, so equivalent mass = 158 / 5 = 31.6. (In neutral medium it is 158 / 3.)

question: The compound CrO5 has a butterfly structure with two peroxide groups. What is the oxidation number of chromium?
why: Two peroxide groups give four O at -1, and one oxide O is -2: total -6. So Cr = +6.

question: 0.635 g of copper reacts completely with excess AgNO3 solution (Cu + 2Ag+ -> Cu2+ + 2Ag). What mass of silver is deposited? (Cu = 63.5, Ag = 108)
why: Cu = 0.01 mol, which displaces 0.02 mol Ag = 2.16 g.

chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
question: What is the IUPAC name of CH3CH2CH2OH?
why: Three carbons make propane, and the -OH is on carbon 1: propan-1-ol.

chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
question: Which functional group is present in aldehydes?
why: Aldehydes carry the -CHO group.

chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
question: How many carbon atoms are present in a molecule of hexane?
why: The prefix hex- means six.

chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
question: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements of atoms are called what?
why: Isomers share a molecular formula but differ in structure.

chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
question: Which of these is a nucleophile?
why: A nucleophile has a lone pair to donate. OH- does; the others are electron-poor.

chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
question: The members CH4, C2H6, C3H8 form a homologous series. What is the difference between successive members?
why: Each member of a homologous series differs from the next by a CH2 unit.

chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
question: What is the IUPAC name of CH3CH2CH(CH3)CH2CH3?
why: The longest chain has five carbons (pentane) with a methyl on carbon 3.

chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
question: How many geometrical isomers are possible for but-2-ene, CH3-CH=CH-CH3?
why: Each double-bond carbon has two different groups, so cis and trans forms exist.

chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
question: Which of these is the strongest acid?
why: More chlorine atoms give a stronger -I effect, which stabilises the carboxylate ion and increases acidity.

chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
question: 0.2 g of an organic compound on complete combustion gives 0.44 g of CO2. What is the percentage of carbon? (C = 12, O = 16)
why: Carbon in CO2 = 0.44 x 12/44 = 0.12 g. Percentage = 0.12 / 0.2 x 100 = 60%.

chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
question: Which method is used to purify a liquid that decomposes below its boiling point?
why: Lowering the pressure lowers the boiling point, so the liquid distils without decomposing.

chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
question: What is the hybridisation of the carbon atom in the nitrile group of CH3-C#N?
why: The nitrile carbon forms one single bond and a triple bond (two sigma bonds), so it is sp hybridised.

chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
question: What is the IUPAC name of CH3-CH(OH)-CH2-CH(CH3)-CH3?
why: Number from the end nearer the -OH, which gets the lowest locant (2). The methyl is on carbon 4.

chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
question: How many structural isomers (alcohols and ethers) are there with the molecular formula C4H10O?
why: There are 4 alcohols and 3 ethers, so 7 in all.

chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
question: How many hyperconjugative structures can be drawn for the isopropyl cation, (CH3)2CH+?
why: Each of the two CH3 groups has 3 alpha C-H bonds, so 2 x 3 = 6 structures.

chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
question: In the Kjeldahl method 0.5 g of a compound gives ammonia that neutralises 20 mL of 0.1 N H2SO4. What is the percentage of nitrogen?
why: Acid used is 2 milli-equivalents, so nitrogen is 2 x 14 = 28 mg. 28 / 500 x 100 = 5.6%.

chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
question: In the Carius method 0.5 g of a bromine compound gives 0.94 g of AgBr. What is the percentage of bromine? (Ag = 108, Br = 80)

chapter: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
question: The sodium fusion extract of a compound containing both nitrogen and sulphur gives a blood-red colour with FeCl3. Which species causes this?
why: During fusion N and S combine with sodium to form NaSCN, which gives Fe(SCN)2+, a blood-red complex.

question: What is formed when ethene is completely hydrogenated?
why: Adding H2 across the double bond with a Ni catalyst gives ethane.

question: Which test shows that a compound is unsaturated?
why: The C=C or C#C bond adds bromine, so the brown colour disappears.

question: What is the hybridisation of each carbon atom in ethyne?
why: Each carbon forms a sigma bond to each neighbour (two regions), so it is sp.

question: What is the IUPAC name of CH3-C#CH?
why: Three carbons with a triple bond: propyne.

question: How many pi electrons are present in the delocalised ring of benzene?
why: Benzene has three double bonds, giving six delocalised pi electrons.

question: What is the shape around each carbon atom of ethene?
why: Each carbon is sp2 hybridised with 120 degree angles, so ethene is planar.

question: Ethene is treated with ozone and then Zn/H2O. What is formed?
why: Ozonolysis cuts the double bond. Each CH2 becomes HCHO, so two methanal molecules form.

question: What is the major product when propene reacts with HBr in the presence of peroxide?
why: The peroxide effect gives anti-Markovnikov addition, so Br attaches to the terminal carbon.

question: Methyl iodide is heated with sodium in dry ether. What is the product?
why: The Wurtz reaction joins two CH3 groups: 2CH3I + 2Na -> CH3-CH3 + 2NaI.

question: Benzene is treated with CH3Cl in the presence of anhydrous AlCl3. What is formed?
why: This is Friedel-Crafts alkylation, so a methyl group replaces one hydrogen of the ring.

question: Which of these gives a white precipitate with ammoniacal silver nitrate?
why: Only terminal alkynes have an acidic hydrogen on the sp carbon. But-2-yne has none.

question: How many different monochloro products (structural isomers) can 2-methylbutane give?
why: 2-Methylbutane has four types of hydrogen: on the two equivalent CH3 groups of C2, on C2 itself, on C3, and on the end CH3 (C4). That gives four products.

question: What is the major product when 2-methylbut-2-ene reacts with HBr?
why: By Markovnikov's rule H goes to the carbon with more hydrogens and Br to the more substituted carbon, giving a tertiary bromide.

question: An alkene on ozonolysis (reductive work-up) gives only propanone and ethanal. What is the alkene?
why: (CH3)2C=CHCH3 breaks into (CH3)2C=O and CH3CHO.

question: How many pi electrons are there in the delocalised system of naphthalene?
why: Naphthalene has five double bonds in its two fused rings, so 10 pi electrons.

question: 10 mL of a gaseous hydrocarbon needs 50 mL of oxygen for complete combustion and gives 30 mL of CO2. What is its formula?
why: Per molecule: 3 C gives 3 CO2. O2 needed = x + y/4 = 5, so y/4 = 2 and y = 8, giving C3H8.

question: Electrolysis of aqueous sodium propanoate (Kolbe) gives mainly which hydrocarbon?
why: Two C2H5 radicals formed at the anode combine to give C2H5-C2H5, butane.

question: But-2-yne is reduced with sodium in liquid ammonia. What is the main product?
why: Na/liquid NH3 gives anti addition of hydrogen, so the trans alkene forms. (Lindlar catalyst gives cis.)
